section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters, petitions, and church or civic resolutions urging President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, scrap iron, oil, machinery, and other war materials to Japan. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could embargo arms only to both China and Japan after a presidential finding of war, did not cover ordinary strategic commodities, and was not being invoked because the administration judged that contrary to broader American interests. The section also contains a vivid missionary account of Japanese bombing casualties at Hankow and Wuchang, correspondence about arms shipments to Germany and Spain, and criticism of European policy toward Czechoslovakia.

keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Letter from Joel S. Johnson urging aid to China
subfiles.about: Johnson asks the President to help China and stop American war supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter argues that China is being systematically devastated by an aggressor while American manufacturers supply ammunition, gas, aircraft, and other war materials to Japan. Johnson suggests that several hundred operational Chinese aircraft could counter Japanese forces on the Yangtze and appeals to Roosevelt's sympathy for China.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of a St. Helena Methodist petition
subfiles.about: Jones transmits a petition from members of the Methodist Church in St. Helena, California.
subfiles.summary: The pastor forwards a petition representing the views of a local Methodist group. She asks Hull to consider it as an expression of the many Americans who share their position.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Neutrality Act and arms exports
subfiles.about: The Department explains why it cannot impose a unilateral arms embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion states that existing law cannot prohibit arms exports to Japan alone and that Roosevelt has decided not to invoke the 1937 Joint Resolution in the Far Eastern conflict. It supplies licensed-export totals for China and Japan and cites Hull's condemnation of civilian bombing and aircraft sales that encourage it.

subfiles.title: Letter from John H. Cowles with clipping on arms exports to Germany
subfiles.about: Cowles thanks Moore for information on neutrality law but argues that American policy enables aggression.
subfiles.summary: Cowles compares the current neutrality regime with American trade during Italy's conquest of Ethiopia and contends that appeasement strengthens dictators such as Mussolini and Hitler. An enclosed clipping reports the National Lawyers Guild's claim that permitted munitions exports to Germany violated the 1921 peace treaty and the neutrality law. Cowles concludes that firmer Anglo-American action could have checked Japan in Manchuria and prevented wider conflict.

subfiles.title: Illegible transmittal enclosing a Hankow hospital letter
subfiles.about: A poorly legible correspondent sends the President material concerning suffering in China and the sale of munitions.
subfiles.summary: The damaged OCR preserves an appeal concerning China's destruction and the moral implications of supplying munitions. The following missionary letter appears to have been enclosed as evidence of conditions under Japanese bombing.

subfiles.title: Gladys Stephenson's account of bombing casualties at Hankow and Wuchang
subfiles.about: Stephenson describes hospital work and civilian suffering during Japanese air raids in central China.
subfiles.summary: Writing from the Methodist General Hospital at Hankow, Stephenson recounts mass casualties at a maternity hospital, refugee shelter, and boat, along with emergency surgery and the terror experienced by wounded children. She reports that fragments of bombs bore American and British markings, says missionaries intend to remain during the expected invasion, and describes shortages of staff. The letter closes with stories of Christian endurance among refugees from Anhui and verses by John Oxenham.

subfiles.title: Inquiry from George B. Leeder about American munitions sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Leeder asks whether American firms supply Japan with munitions and aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Leeder explains that Indian acquaintances expect him, as an American citizen, to know whether the reports are true. He notes strong Indian sympathy for China, the failure of Nehru's proposed boycott of Japanese goods, and his own hope that any American aircraft sales will cease.

subfiles.title: Instructions to the American consul at Karachi for answering Leeder
subfiles.about: The Department supplies a proposed explanation of American arms-export law for transmission to George B. Leeder.
subfiles.summary: The instruction says that a presidential finding of war would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while no law permits stopping exports to Japan alone in the absence of such a proclamation. It describes the Department's advisory policy against aircraft sales to countries bombing civilians and says manufacturers generally cooperate. It also explains why Roosevelt has not invoked the Neutrality Act and gives licensed-export totals for both belligerents.

subfiles.title: China Club of Seattle appeal against war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.from: W. E. Priestley, China Club of Seattle
subfiles.about: Priestley argues that supplying Japan strengthens a potential American enemy and weakens China.
subfiles.summary: The letter portrays China as fighting both for itself and indirectly for American security in the Pacific. It calls for helping China break Japan's militarism and invokes the bombing of the Panay as a warning about American scrap iron reaching Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. E. Priestley
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains the legal limits on stopping arms and scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that invoking the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan and that the President considers such action contrary to the country's broader interests. It gives licensed-export totals and emphasizes that scrap iron is not classified as an arm or implement of war. Consequently, neither the President nor the Secretary of State possesses statutory authority to prohibit its export.

subfiles.title: Cumberland County WCTU transmittal
subfiles.about: Kast forwards a resolution adopted by the Cumberland County Woman's Christian Temperance Union.
subfiles.summary: Kast writes in her capacity as the organization's representative. The enclosed resolution concerns American material and financial support for Japan's war in China.

subfiles.title: Cumberland County WCTU resolution against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: Cumberland County Woman's Christian Temperance Union
subfiles.about: The organization asks the government to prevent American resources from aiding Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The resolution alleges that roughly half of Japan's war essentials come from the United States and that ending those imports could compel a withdrawal from China. It declares that Americans cannot economically support conduct they morally condemn and demands action against direct or indirect aid.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Ida G. Kast
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost answers the WCTU resolution by outlining the Neutrality Act and its limitations.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, not Japan alone, and that Roosevelt has chosen not to invoke the law. It presents licensed-export totals and notes that ordinary commodities cannot be prohibited under the Neutrality Act. Copies of the Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Oberlin petition against munitions shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Clarence H. Hamilton, Lulu S. Hamilton, Ruth Hamilton, and Miriam Hamilton
subfiles.about: The Hamiltons urge action to stop American munitions and war supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: The signers say that a year of war has convinced them that American supplies materially sustain Japan's campaign in China. They characterize Japanese action as contrary to democratic principles expressed in Hull's own speeches and request prompt corrective action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Clarence H. Hamilton
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains why American law does not permit an arms embargo directed solely at Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply repeats that the Joint Resolution would bar shipments to both belligerents following a presidential war finding. It says Roosevelt has decided that invocation would not serve American interests, gives comparative license totals, and distinguishes statutory arms from other commodities. The Joint Resolution and an arms-traffic pamphlet are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner's transmittal to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hiltner sends Hull a copy of his letter to President Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner says the enclosed letter reflects strong regional opposition to continuing shipments of war materials to Japan. He also notes that it conveys local reaction to recent European events.

subfiles.title: Hiltner's letter to President Roosevelt on Japan and Czechoslovakia
subfiles.about: Hiltner demands an end to trade supporting Japan and condemns the impending dismemberment of Czechoslovakia.
subfiles.summary: Writing as chairman of the Committee Against International Aggression, Hiltner calls American war-material shipments to Japan a national disgrace and urges Roosevelt to pressure exporters and deny financing for conquered territories. He then denounces British and French treatment of Czechoslovakia and the participation of an American ambassador in the negotiations. He asks American officials to avoid complicity while keeping the country out of European war.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Walter G. Hiltner
subfiles.about: Yost refers Hiltner to an earlier explanation and describes the Department's stand against civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: The reply points to a May 2 letter explaining the nonapplication of the Neutrality Act to the Far Eastern conflict. It adds that the government has repeatedly condemned civilian bombing and directly advised American aircraft manufacturers and exporters accordingly, while stressing that such advisory intervention is exceptional.

subfiles.title: Signed Auburndale petition for a comprehensive embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Paul Rowland and other American citizens
subfiles.about: The signers request an embargo on arms and strategic raw materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition commends Hull for discouraging sales of bombing planes but argues that words must be followed by stronger action against Japanese attacks on Chinese civilians. It proposes stopping oil, steel, scrap iron, cotton, trucks, aircraft parts, and other military supplies, and publicizing firms that continue the trade. The signers contend that otherwise America becomes Japan's economic partner in aggression.

subfiles.title: Paul Rowland's letter to Francis B. Sayre
subfiles.about: Rowland presses Sayre for concrete action against exports sustaining Japan's war machine.
subfiles.summary: Rowland encloses the June petition and praises Hull's recent broadcast while insisting that American principles require practical enforcement. He proposes an immediate official request to stop all useful exports to Japan and publication of the names of noncompliant firms. Comparing the Axis powers' conduct to repeated bluffing, he cites Czechoslovakia's May resistance as an example of firmness.

subfiles.title: Copy of June 20 Auburndale embargo petition
subfiles.from: Paul Rowland and other American citizens
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the appeal for a complete embargo on military supplies and raw materials sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites continued Japanese bombing and machine-gunning of Chinese noncombatants despite American protests. It urges restrictions on arms, oil, steel, scrap iron, copper, cotton, trucks, and aircraft parts, together with public identification of firms that persist in the trade.

subfiles.title: Francis B. Sayre's reply to Paul Rowland
subfiles.about: Sayre acknowledges Rowland's August letter and the copy of the June petition.
subfiles.summary: Sayre says he has returned to Washington and found Rowland's correspondence awaiting him. He expresses interest in Rowland's views on Japan and offers warm personal regards without addressing the requested policy changes in detail.

subfiles.title: Interim acknowledgment of Paul Rowland's letter
subfiles.about: Sayre's secretary acknowledges Rowland's letter while Sayre is on vacation.
subfiles.summary: The secretary confirms receipt of the August 17 letter and its copy of the June 20 appeal to Hull. Rowland is told that the material will be brought to Sayre's attention after his return in early September.

subfiles.title: Louisa S. Neumann's transmittal of a ten-person petition
subfiles.about: Neumann forwards a petition from ten people opposing American support for Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Neumann describes the subject as tremendously important and trusts that it will receive the President's attention. The letter is written in her capacity as executive secretary of the International Institute of the Providence YWCA.

subfiles.title: Providence petition to end trade supporting Japanese aggression
subfiles.from: Louisa S. Neumann and other signers
subfiles.about: The petition asks Roosevelt to use every practical means to end American trade that supports Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The signers invoke the Nine-Power Treaty, Kellogg Pact, civilian bombing, and American supplies of aircraft, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks. They express support for an independent democratic China and condemn profits derived from Japanese aggression. The appeal frames an end to the trade as consistent with Roosevelt's Good Neighbor principle and the interests of Americans, Chinese, and Japanese alike.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Louisa S. Neumann
subfiles.about: Yost answers the petition with the Department's standard explanation of neutrality law and aircraft-export policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply says a presidential finding of war would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no authority exists to target Japan alone. It explains Roosevelt's decision not to invoke the law, presents comparative license totals, and distinguishes arms from unregulated commodities. Yost also notes the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and its direct representations to aircraft manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Lulu Jackson Clymer's appeal concerning America's share in Japan's war
subfiles.about: Clymer asks what the government can do to stop the United States from serving as Japan's arsenal.
subfiles.summary: She argues that American machinery, machine tools, oil, pig iron, and scrap iron make the country a virtual partner in Japan's war against China. Her Columbus group is organizing education, study, personal boycotts, and other efforts to assist China. She expresses confidence in Roosevelt and Hull while urging stronger government action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lulu Jackson Clymer
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains that the Neutrality Act does not authorize restrictions on the non-arms commodities Clymer identified.
subfiles.summary: The reply says machinery, oil, and iron fall outside the Act's limited definition of arms and that no presidential war finding has been made. Arms exports therefore remain subject to licensing rather than prohibition, with special provisions applying to China. Yost adds that Roosevelt considers invocation of the Joint Resolution contrary to the country's overall interests.

subfiles.title: West Virginia church conference transmittal
subfiles.about: Knight forwards resolutions adopted by the West Virginia Conference of the Church of the United Brethren in Christ.
subfiles.summary: Writing for the Committee on Foreign Missions, Knight encloses the conference's resolutions and asks that they receive careful consideration. The accompanying material addresses war supplies, China relief, and the coming missionary conference at Madras.

subfiles.title: West Virginia Conference resolutions on war materials, China relief, and Madras
subfiles.from: West Virginia Conference, Church of the United Brethren in Christ
subfiles.to: President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The resolutions oppose American war-material sales, support China relief, and endorse the 1938 Madras missionary conference.
subfiles.summary: The first resolution asks the government to end traffic making Americans partners in the destruction of national independence and civilian life. The second urges church cooperation with nationwide China relief after a disappointing Red Cross campaign. The third calls for prayer and cooperation surrounding the December World Missionary Conference in Madras and subsequent North American meetings.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. M. Knight
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the church resolutions and summarizes the government's position on civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Knight for copies of the conference resolutions. Addressing the first resolution, Yost says Hull has repeatedly condemned civilian bombing and that the government conveyed this position directly to aircraft manufacturers and exporters. Copies of the Joint Resolution and the arms-traffic pamphlet are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Alice E. Frame's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Frame asks Roosevelt to stop American support for Japan's aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: Frame praises Roosevelt personally but argues that Americans bear responsibility because Japan obtains vital supplies from the United States. She quotes Mussolini's newspaper mocking the contrast between American peace speeches and American armament exports. She presents withholding aid from Japan as the minimum support due China's struggle for liberty.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Alice E. Frame
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains the government's legal and policy reasons for not imposing a unilateral embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the Joint Resolution would prohibit arms shipments to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding of war. Roosevelt has declined to invoke it in view of broader national interests, and the Department supplies comparative arms-license totals. Yost further explains that the Act does not authorize restrictions on commodities outside the proclaimed arms list.

subfiles.title: Note outlining questions about American war-material exports
subfiles.about: The note lists questions about American materials supplied to Japan, Nazi Germany, and Fascist Italy.
subfiles.summary: The fragment asks about America's share in Japan's war guilt and whether American materials sent to Germany and Italy are transshipped onward. The fuller version of these questions appears in M. Levi's following letter.

subfiles.title: M. Levi's letter on war supplies to Japan and Franco's forces
subfiles.about: Levi asks about American responsibility for supplying Japan and possible transshipment of arms to Franco's forces in Spain.
subfiles.summary: Levi cites the claim that America provides 54 percent of Japan's war material and asks whether supplies sent to Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy reach General Franco. He calls such trade profitable but morally tainted and argues that government foreign policy does not reflect the democratic conscience of the American people.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to M. Levi
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost answers Levi's questions about the Far East and alleged arms transshipment to Spanish rebels.
subfiles.summary: The reply gives the standard explanation that the Neutrality Act cannot embargo Japan alone and that Roosevelt has not invoked it for the Sino-Japanese conflict. It provides arms-license totals and distinguishes listed arms from other commodities. Regarding Spain, it says export licenses must name the ultimate destination and that the Department has no evidence of American arms reaching the rebel forces directly or indirectly since the Spanish embargo took effect.

subfiles.title: Presbytery of Columbus resolution on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Patterson reports a Presbyterian resolution urging immediate action against exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Presbytery of Columbus adopted the measure at its fall meeting in Lancaster and directed Patterson to send it to Hull for presentation to Roosevelt. The resolution says American exports have assisted Japan's destruction of Chinese life and property and calls for speedy, effective restrictions.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frank M. Patterson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost responds to the Presbytery's resolution by describing the limitations of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that a war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that no legal authority exists for a Japan-only embargo. It says Roosevelt has declined invocation in light of national interests and that ordinary commodities fall outside the law. Comparative values of licensed arms exports to China and Japan are also provided.

subfiles.title: Katherine S. Blake's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Blake urges Roosevelt to halt scrap-iron sales and other American aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Blake describes civilian deaths, battlefield casualties, and Japanese narcotics activity in China while criticizing the United States as Japan's principal supplier. She cites Wellington Koo's speech before the League of Nations and contrasts the restriction on helium sales to Germany with the continued export of scrap iron to Japan. She appeals to Roosevelt as a source of international hope.

subfiles.title: Southern California Christian resolution for nonparticipation in aggression
subfiles.from: S. M. Bernard and Ollie S. Mason
subfiles.about: A church convention resolution demands an end to shipments usable by Japan's military and assistance for China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution says American aircraft, gasoline, munitions, raw materials, and machinery facilitate the bombardment of Chinese cities and civilian suffering. It condemns profiting from that trade while protesting Japanese conduct as hypocritical. The convention urges a policy of nonparticipation in aggression, an immediate halt to relevant shipments to Japan, and peaceful assistance to China; Baldwin Park Christian Church subsequently authorized the submission.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to S. M. Bernard
subfiles.about: Yost answers the Baldwin Park resolution by explaining neutrality law and the aircraft-export advisory policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges the request to stop all goods usable by aggressor forces and to aid China. It repeats that the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan, cannot regulate ordinary commodities, and has not been invoked because of broader American interests. Yost supplies arms-license totals and notes the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and its representations to aircraft exporters.

subfiles.title: S. Warren Sturgis's proposal for voluntary export restrictions
subfiles.about: Sturgis asks why Hull cannot request an end to war-material exports and publicize exporters who refuse.
subfiles.summary: Recalling earlier correspondence about the lack of congressional authority for compulsory restrictions, Sturgis proposes extending Hull's aircraft policy to all war materials. He believes publicity could greatly reduce the trade and quotes a purported Japanese representative who mocks American morality as subordinate to profit.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the Sturgis draft reply
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains the precedent used in drafting a reply to Sturgis.
subfiles.summary: The writer says the second paragraph closely follows language used in a September 20 response to Congressman Tinkham. The constituent's question in that earlier exchange is described as markedly similar to Sturgis's proposal.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles's request for a draft reply to Sturgis
subfiles.about: Welles asks Hamilton to draft an appropriate response to his former Groton master.
subfiles.summary: Welles identifies Sturgis as one of his former masters at Groton School. He requests a reply and specifies that the salutation should be addressed to “Mr. Sturgis.”

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles's reply to S. Warren Sturgis
subfiles.about: Welles explains why the Department's advisory action against aircraft exports is treated as exceptional.
subfiles.summary: Welles says the aircraft request rested on the government's unequivocal condemnation of bombing civilian populations. He states that only in exceptional cases does the Department intervene through such nonstatutory advice. Although he does not adopt Sturgis's broader proposal, he acknowledges its motives sympathetically.

subfiles.title: Henry H. Welles's appeal for legislation against war supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Welles asks Roosevelt to support measures prohibiting American financial and material aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles argues that growing numbers of Americans recognize their country's share in Japan's war guilt through credits and war materials. He says public opinion increasingly supports Roosevelt's opposition to Japanese aggression and asks for legislation at the next congressional session or faster executive action under existing law. He distinguishes the Japanese people from the military clique responsible for aggression in China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Henry H. Welles
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Welles's proposal and begins explaining the absence of authority for a unilateral arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The reply says Welles's comments will receive appropriate attention. It explains that no statute permits the President to prohibit arms exports to one belligerent but not the other and encloses the May 1, 1937 Joint Resolution. The document continues beyond this section.
